screens.title: DirectionalLight3D
screens.narratorSegment: DirectionalLight3D models light that comes from infinitely far away so its rays are parallel and only its rotation affects illumination. This makes it ideal for outdoor or global lighting where position does not change the result. A common practical use is the sun in an outdoor scene: rotating the light changes the time of day and shadow direction without moving the node in world space. Key properties to tune are Color, Energy, and whether shadows are enabled. For example, reduce Energy at sunset to keep highlights warm but dim overall intensity. A frequent misconception is to try to position the directional light near the scene; position is ignored — only rotation matters. Another mistake is enabling high-quality real-time shadows for every directional light without testing performance. Try this concrete example: add a DirectionalLight3D to a small scene, rotate it to a low angle to simulate sunset, enable shadow_enabled, and observe long soft shadows. Check the shadow bias if you see self-shadowing artifacts. Takeaway: use DirectionalLight3D for wide, even lighting and drive day-night changes by rotation rather than position. What sun angle will best highlight your scene's silhouette?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › DirectionalLight3D
Core idea

Parallel rays, rotation controls angle

Directional lights simulate distant sources. Position is ignored; rotation and intensity determine shadows and highlights across the entire scene.

Properties to tune
  • Color — tint of the light.
  • Energy — overall intensity.
  • Specular — contribution to reflective highlights.
  • shadow_enabled — whether the light casts shadows.
Key Takeaway
Use DirectionalLight3D to set global sun/moon lighting and animate rotation to create day-night cycles.
Concrete example
Add one DirectionalLight3D and rotate its X to 45 degrees for midday, 15 degrees for sunrise/sunset. Enable shadows for a dramatic silhouette effect; reduce energy to avoid blown highlights at sunset.
Common Mistake
Moving the directional light's position to try to change lighting. Rotation only matters; repositioning has no visual impact.

screens.title: OmniLight3D (Point Light)
screens.narratorSegment: OmniLight3D emits light equally in all directions from a single point in space, much like a physical light bulb. Its intensity falls off with distance, so nearby objects receive strong illumination while distant objects are dimmer. Important settings include Color and Energy, but also parameters that control attenuation and range so you can limit the light's influence. A typical use is a torch or lamp placed near geometry to light a small region. A helpful example: place an OmniLight3D above a table to illuminate nearby objects while leaving the room corners darker. A common misconception is to expect uniform lighting across the whole level — instead, plan placements so falloff contributes to contrast and mood. For shadows, enabling shadow_enabled will let the OmniLight3D cast local shadows, but remember that multiple shadowed Omni lights multiply cost. Takeaway: use OmniLight3D to add local warmth or highlights, and control its range to avoid unintended global lighting. Which parts of your scene need local detail and which should remain in ambient shadow? OmniLight3D (Point Light) means use omnilight3d for localized, warm sources; manage range and falloff to protect global mood and performance.. In practical terms, local, omnidirectional light with distance falloff. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › OmniLight3D (Point Light)
How it works

OmniLight3D emits equally in all directions and uses distance-based falloff. Tune range so the effect is local rather than globally brightening the scene.

When to use
Torches, lamps, candles, or any small source where proximity matters.
Tuning tips
  • Lower range to keep illumination local.
  • Adjust Energy so it complements ambient light.
  • Enable shadows selectively only for key Omni lights.
Concrete scenario
Place an OmniLight3D above a campfire object with low range and warm color. The fire lights nearby characters while the forest beyond remains darker, preserving contrast.
Common Mistake
Adding many Omni lights with shadows enabled everywhere, causing excessive GPU cost and muddy lighting. Prefer a few shadowed sources and simpler lights elsewhere.
Key Takeaway
Use Omni lights for localized highlights; tune falloff and enable shadows only where they matter.

screens.title: SpotLight3D
screens.narratorSegment: SpotLight3D emits light in a cone, making it perfect for flashlights, headlights, or stage lights. Its cone angle and range define how wide and how far the light reaches, and you can often animate the angle for effects like spreading or narrowing beams. Like other Light3D nodes, it has Color, Energy, and Specular controls, and can cast shadows. A concrete example is a flashlight attached to a player: use a narrow cone and limited range so the beam only illuminates nearby surfaces, improving performance. Be mindful of a common misconception: widening the cone to cover more area might appear convenient but dramatically increases the number of affected surfaces and can raise G P U cost, especially with shadows. Tuning the inner and outer cone and falloff allows you to craft a soft-edged beam. Takeaway: SpotLight3D is the right choice when you need a directional, sculpted light area; keep angle and range tight to preserve performance. How will you use cone softness to shape your beam's edge? SpotLight3D means use spotlight3d for precisely aimed beams; control cone angle and falloff to limit lighting cost and shape edges.. In practical terms, directed cone light for focused illumination. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › SpotLight3D
Core concept

Cone-shaped, directional illumination

Spot lights create focused beams that can be softened at the edges. Adjust inner/outer cone and range for desired effect.

Use cases
Flashlights, car headlights, stage spotlights, and any directed beam effect.
Performance tip
Narrow cones and short ranges reduce the number of lit fragments and shadow cost.
Concrete example
Attach a SpotLight3D to a vehicle's headlamp with a tight cone and limited range. Add a soft outer cone to avoid harsh edges while keeping the scene readable at night.
Common Mistake
Widening cone indiscriminately to light a large area. This increases shading and shadowing costs quickly; prefer multiple local lights or ambient tweaks instead.

screens.title: Light Properties & Shadows
screens.narratorSegment: All Light3D nodes share core properties: Color, Energy, and Specular. Color sets the tint, Energy controls brightness, and Specular determines contribution to highlights on shiny materials. Crucially, each light also offers shadow controls; enabling shadows adds depth and object separation, but at a computational cost. Godot provides shadow modes like ShadowMapping and PCF variants to trade quality for performance. A concrete example is enabling soft PCF shadows for one primary directional light to get pleasing penumbras while leaving other lights shadowless or using cheaper shadows. A common misconception is that shadows always improve visuals; in some scenes, weak or noisy shadows can reduce clarity. Another common problem is shadow artifacts like shadow acne caused by self-shadowing; bias settings help but must be tuned to avoid peter-panning where shadows separate from their caster. Takeaway: treat shadows as a design decision—prioritize primary lights for high-quality shadows and use bias and mode settings to control artifacts. Which lights in your scene truly need shadows? keyIdea.text: Shadows add realism but cost performance; choose modes and bias carefully and reserve high-quality shadows for primary lights.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Light Properties & Shadows
Shared light properties
  • Color — tint that mixes with materials.
  • Energy — intensity of illumination.
  • Specular — amount of reflective highlights.
Shadow controls
Enable shadow_enabled to cast shadows. Choose shadow Mode (e.g., basic ShadowMapping or PCF variants) and adjust Bias to reduce self-shadowing artifacts.
Example tuning
For a primary sun, use PCF7 or PCF13 for softer shadows and tune bias to avoid acne. For decorative lamps, consider disabling shadows or using a low-cost shadow mode.
Common Issues
  • Shadow acne — visible self-shadowing artifacts; fix with bias.
  • Peter-panning — too much bias separates shadows from casters; balance is key.
Key Takeaway
Quality shadows for main lights, cheaper or no shadows for fill lights keeps visuals and performance balanced.

screens.title: Avoiding Shadow Artifacts
screens.narratorSegment: Shadow artifacts are a common source of frustration, but they are predictable and solvable. The main artifact, shadow acne, happens when surfaces self-shadow because the shadow map precision causes the surface to compare as occluded. The standard mitigation is adjusting Bias settings — a small offset that reduces self-occlusion — but bias is a delicate tool: too little and acne remains, too much and you get peter-panning where shadows appear detached from casters. Godot's shadow modes offer additional trade-offs: simpler shadow mapping is cheaper but sharper, while PCF7 and PCF13 produce softer edges at higher cost. A step-by-step approach is effective: first, enable shadows only on the primary light and test for artifacts; second, increase bias incrementally until acne reduces; third, if shadows become detached, reduce bias and consider increasing normal bias or using a softer PCF mode to mask small errors. Another practical fix is moving the light slightly or adjusting caster geometry to remove near-zero thickness faces. Takeaway: tune bias and shadow mode iteratively and always test on target hardware. When you encounter acne, which adjustment will you try first: bias or mode?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Avoiding Shadow Artifacts
Iterative tuning process
Step 1
Enable shadows for the main light first and observe artifacts.
Step 2
Incrementally adjust Bias until acne reduces—but watch for peter-panning.
Step 3
If detachment appears, lower Bias and try a softer PCF mode or geometry fixes.
Quick fixes
  • Adjust normal bias where available.
  • Avoid extremely thin geometry that self-intersects.
Testing tip
Test on target hardware with multiple lights enabled to measure real performance impact.

screens.title: Performance Strategies for Lighting
screens.narratorSegment: Real-time lighting and shadows are among the most expensive operations in a 3D renderer. The key is to allocate cost to where the player notices it most. Begin by identifying primary lights that shape composition — usually a directional sun or a main indoor key light — and give them better shadow quality. For secondary and decorative lights, consider disabling shadows or using lower-cost modes. Another common strategy is to limit the number of shadow-casting lights affecting a single object. Baking static lighting or lightmaps can be used for non-dynamic elements to preserve high visual quality with negligible runtime cost, but baking has limits for dynamic or movable objects. In practice, profile your scene: enable and disable shadows and measure frame rate on your target device. A concrete workflow is: enable high-quality shadow for directional light only, use Omni/Spot without shadows for minor fixtures, and bake static shadows into textures for complex static props. Takeaway: distribute shadow cost intentionally and test on target hardware. Which light will you reserve for real-time shadows first in your scene? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Performance Strategies for Lighting
Decision checklist
  • Identify main lights that affect composition and give them priority.
  • Disable shadows for decorative lights or use cheaper shadow modes.
  • Consider baking static lighting where possible for complex static geometry.
  • Limit how many shadow-casting lights affect the same object.
Concrete workflow
Primary directional: high-quality shadows. Secondary lamp: no shadows or low-cost shadow. Static props: bake shadows into lightmaps.
Testing
Profile on target hardware and iterate. Visual quality must be weighed against framerate goals.

screens.title: WorldEnvironment and Environment Resource
screens.narratorSegment: The WorldEnvironment node holds an Environment resource that controls global rendering settings for a scene. Typically you should have one WorldEnvironment per scene that you intend to render uniformly. The Environment resource centralizes background settings, ambient light, fog, glow, and color adjustments so that a single place defines the scene's overall look. Background can be a solid color, a Sky resource, or even a CanvasTexture for stylized needs. Ambient Light provides non-directional base illumination that prevents purely black occluded areas; use it to lift dark corners without removing important contrast from direct lights. Fog adds atmospheric depth by obscuring distant objects; it has parameters for color, depth, and height to shape how quickly objects fade with distance. Glow creates bloom around bright emissive areas. A common mistake is leaving the environment unconfigured, which can make a properly lit scene look flat or too dark. Takeaway: treat the Environment resource as your scene's visual master control and adjust its properties to match the mood and hardware constraints. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Dynamic Control with GDScript
Script concept

Rotate the DirectionalLight3D over time to simulate the sun moving. Use a time-derived value to modulate fog settings for atmospheric variation.

Why this matters
Dynamic changes make worlds feel alive and allow night/day transitions without reauthoring scene assets.
Example code
# Example: Dynamically adjusting light and environment properties
extends Node3D

@onready var directional_light = $DirectionalLight3D
@onready var world_environment = $WorldEnvironment

func _process(delta):
  # Rotate the directional light to simulate a day-night cycle
  directional_light.rotation_degrees.x += 0.1 * delta # Rotate around X-axis

  # Adjust fog based on time (simple example)
  var time_of_day = fmod(OS.get_unix_time_from_datetime(OS.get_datetime()), 24.0 * 3600.0) # Seconds in a day
  var fog_intensity = sin(time_of_day / (24.0 * 3600.0) * PI) # Peaks at midday, low at night

  if world_environment and world_environment.environment:
    world_environment.environment.fog_enabled = true
    world_environment.environment.fog_depth_begin = 10.0 + (1.0 - fog_intensity) * 50.0 # Thicker fog at night
    world_environment.environment.fog_color = Color(0.7, 0.8, 0.9, fog_intensity * 0.5) # Bluer, more opaque fog at night
Key Takeaway
Small runtime changes to light rotation and environment parameters produce convincing dynamic atmospheres with minimal asset work.

Lighting is one of the fastest ways to change how a 3D scene feels. In this chapter we focus on Godot's Light3D types — Directional, Omni, and Spot — and on the WorldEnvironment resource that controls sky, fog, ambient light, and post-processing. You'll learn how each light type behaves, how shadows add depth but cost performance, and how a properly configured environment resource unifies ambient and background settings so your scene stays readable. We'll also cover two sky approaches: a procedural physical sky and a panorama sky, and how fog and ambient light influence visibility and mood. As you follow along you will practice placing lights, enabling shadows selectively, and editing Environment parameters to move a scene from flat and dark to clear, moody, or cinematic. A practical code snippet demonstrates how to drive a day-night cycle by rotating a directional light and varying fog. By the end, you'll be able to pick the right light type for a need, protect performance, and use WorldEnvironment to control global atmosphere. Consider how subtle shifts in ambient energy or fog depth can completely change player perception; which mood do you want to achieve first?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure Godot's common Light3D types so they serve specific design needs, implement shadows with sensible quality/performance trade-offs, and control global atmosphere with the WorldEnvironment resource. Specifically, you will learn how DirectionalLight3D simulates sun and moonlight by rotation alone; when to use OmniLight3D as a local point source and how its falloff affects nearby geometry; and how SpotLight3D shapes illumination using cone angle and range. You will also understand how shadow modes and bias settings reduce artifacts, and why enabling high-quality shadows on every light is usually a bad idea for performance. Finally, you will create and tune an Environment resource: set Background with a Sky, adjust Ambient Light to fill dark corners, and configure Fog and Glow to craft mood. These skills let you move a scene from flat and unreadable to expressive and atmospheric on target hardware. Think about a small outdoor scene: which light will you pick for the sun, which for a lamp, and how will you use ambient energy to preserve shadow detail?

This second objectives slide focuses on practical application. You will create a 3D test scene with a ground plane and a few meshes, add a WorldEnvironment and Environment resource, and iteratively tune DirectionalLight3D rotation and intensity to simulate times of day. You will also practice enabling shadows only for the primary light and compare shadow Mode and Bias settings to recognize common artifacts like shadow acne. Then you will add an OmniLight3D or SpotLight3D near objects to see local lighting effects and use Ambient Light to gently lift dark corners without washing out primary light contrast. Finally, you will switch the Environment Background between a PhysicalSkyMaterial for dynamic scattering and a PanoramaSkyMaterial to evaluate photorealistic lighting. This hands-on flow ensures the skills are tied to choices and testing on target hardware, reinforcing the difference between visual quality and runtime cost. After practicing, reflect on which light produced the clearest silhouette and which environment tweak most improved readability.

DirectionalLight3D models light that comes from infinitely far away so its rays are parallel and only its rotation affects illumination. This makes it ideal for outdoor or global lighting where position does not change the result. A common practical use is the sun in an outdoor scene: rotating the light changes the time of day and shadow direction without moving the node in world space. Key properties to tune are Color, Energy, and whether shadows are enabled. For example, reduce Energy at sunset to keep highlights warm but dim overall intensity. A frequent misconception is to try to position the directional light near the scene; position is ignored — only rotation matters. Another mistake is enabling high-quality real-time shadows for every directional light without testing performance. Check the shadow bias if you see self-shadowing artifacts. Takeaway: use DirectionalLight3D for wide, even lighting and drive day-night changes by rotation rather than position. OmniLight3D emits light equally in all directions from a single point in space, much like a physical light bulb. Its intensity falls off with distance, so nearby objects receive strong illumination while distant objects are dimmer. Important settings include Color and Energy, but also parameters that control attenuation and range so you can limit the light's influence. A typical use is a torch or lamp placed near geometry to light a small region. A helpful example: place an OmniLight3D above a table to illuminate nearby objects while leaving the room corners darker. SpotLight3D emits light in a cone, making it perfect for flashlights, headlights, or stage lights. Its cone angle and range define how wide and how far the light reaches, and you can often animate the angle for effects like spreading or narrowing beams. Like other Light3D nodes, it has Color, Energy, and Specular controls, and can cast shadows. A concrete example is a flashlight attached to a player: use a narrow cone and limited range so the beam only illuminates nearby surfaces, improving performance. These are the essential takeaways to keep in mind. DirectionalLight3D simulates distant light — rotation controls direction, not position. OmniLight3D is a local point source with falloff, useful for lamps and torches. SpotLight3D gives a cone-shaped beam for focused effects such as flashlights. Shadows improve realism but cost performance; choose shadow modes and bias carefully and reserve high-quality shadows for primary lights.
